item.text: {"text":"Recent work supports combining sequence encoders with explicit item transitions. [DTR4Rec (2024/2025)](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10489-024-05875-3) builds long-window directed transition counts and short-window co-occurrence counts, then learns their fusion with sequential predictions. [TGCL4SR (AAAI 2024)](https://ojs.aaai.org/index.php/AAAI/article/view/28789) combines a global temporal item-transition graph with a Transformer using time intervals; graph contrastive learning adds complexity. A lightweight alternative, [Revisiting Graph Projections (2025)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.09209), derives a directed weighted product graph from user–item interactions, making graph projection a useful baseline before introducing deeper graph networks.\n\nComplementarity requires more than lexical similarity: [SComGNN (AAAI 2024)](https://ojs.aaai.org/index.php/AAAI/article/view/28734) models both relevance and dissimilarity using low- and mid-frequency graph filters. However, transition direction alone does not identify substitutes, compatibility, or unmet needs; these remain hypotheses without relation labels. For this constrained benchmark, a plausible synthesis—not a verified published recipe—is a SASRec residual scorer using separate source/target embeddings, smoothed directed transition weights, and a small title/description token encoder trained from scratch. Text could share statistical strength across sparse items, while asymmetric scoring preserves follow-on direction. Validate graph-only, text-only, and fused variants using the common macro HR@10; treat learned edges as predictive associations rather than established complement/substitute labels."}
